prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms held at a magic wavelength opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from a two-part prize (B049 plus B047) to B049 alone, for Katori and Ye. The first-round exchange did what it should: it tested the second part and it did not hold. B049 has the broadest and most stable support on the shortlist, six of eight round-1 configurations name it, and the scientific case has survived every question put to it. The idea is a single, identifiable mechanism, the magic wavelength that cancels the lattice light shift so that thousands of neutral atoms are interrogated Doppler- and recoil-free. The realisation moved fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18, and the result has been reproduced independently at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB and SYRTE and checked by clock comparisons between sites. As an instrument builder I weigh that last point most: the systematics are understood in detail and the number is reproduced by groups that do not share a cryostat, so it will last. The citation should name the concept and its realisation, not applications, because the redefinition of the second is still pending and the geodesy and constants-testing harvest is partly prospective. I do not make the redefinition a precondition.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still the one raised by Danielsson, Eriksson and Olsson: this is a measurement capability rather than a surprise about nature, and the 2005 comb prize and 2012 ion-control prize cover the lineage. I answer the overlap by framing: neither earlier prize covers many-atom interrogation at a magic wavelength, which is a different mechanism with a different systematics budget, but the committee has to state that boundary in the citation and the background text. The attribution to Ye is the second weakness. Olsson is right that Katori holds the proposal and first realisation, and that Ye's role is partly taking the platform to record accuracy and studying density and many-body shifts, which a purist could call a better second wave. Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, Lisdat, Ludlow and others are outside the two names. I cannot settle priority from the supplied material. Finally, no measured departure from expectation (time dilation anomaly, drifting constants) has yet appeared, so the discovery content is performance and new capability, and I accept that this is a judgement and not a fact.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Katori alone would be the more defensible attribution, since Ye's role is largely taking the lattice platform to record accuracy and many-body physics, and asks that the citation say the invention and realisation are the discovery and not a lifetime award.
responses.response: I agree with the wording point and have adopted it: my citation is confined to the invention and realisation of the lattice clock, with no list of applications. On keeping Ye, my view is that a clock is not demonstrated by the proposal. The realisation includes showing that density shifts, blackbody shifts and lattice light shifts can be controlled at the 1e-18 level, and that is what convinced the community the scheme works. That was done in Ye's laboratory, and it was done in the same period as the first Katori realisations, not decades later. So I count it as part of the realisation, not a later execution of someone else's idea. I would, however, accept Katori alone as a fallback if the atomic specialists, Lindroth and Kroll, judged Ye's contribution to be refinement. I defer to them on that priority question, and I would not hold up the prize on it.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B049 eighth because the discovery content is so far a null result on constants and a promise on geodesy, and he notes that the 2005 and 2012 prizes cover much of the conceptual ground. He also holds B024 as thin in breadth of support but clean in science.
responses.response: The discovery-versus-instrument concern is fair and I do not dismiss it. As an experimentalist I would answer that new instruments are a legitimate prize category when they open a regime that was inaccessible, and a 1e-18 neutral-atom clock compared across continents is that. I also share your wish for a measured surprise, but I do not think the prize should wait for one. On B024, I still hold it as my first alternative, as the cleanest discovery from nature. I would not lead with it: three named spokespersons for Daya Bay and RENO leave out Double Chooz and the accelerator appearance results, and the committee would need to explain why theta-13 is distinct from the 2015 prize. If the committee finds B049 too much of a tool, B024 is where I would go, and your own caution about its breadth of support is why it is a fallback and not my lead.

responses.point: Lindroth declines to pair IceCube with the clocks until someone with astroparticle expertise shows that Halzen alone carries the credit, and she argues that the citation should say what is new, many atoms trapped at the magic wavelength, and not just a better optical clock.
responses.response: Your challenge on B047 is the one I could not answer, and I am the member with the astroparticle expertise you ask for. I cannot document from the supplied material that Halzen alone is the decisive credit. The AMANDA lineage, the other founders and spokespersons, and the analyses behind TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 mean that a one-person part would be a statement about leadership of a collaboration of hundreds, and the source identifications rest on one instrument. I therefore withdraw B047 from my configuration and do not make it an alternative either. I also adopt your citation framing and have written the magic-wavelength, many-atom point into it explicitly.

responses.point: Eriksson holds B048 first, arguing that Kane-Mele Z2 theory plus Molenkamp's HgTe experiment is a compact, mature line, and says that B049 needs a stronger case that something new is learned about nature given two earlier precision prizes.
responses.response: I defer to you on the condensed-matter physics, and I take the maturity argument seriously: fifteen years of independent confirmation is real. My difficulty with B048 remains attribution. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe realisation that Molenkamp tested, and Zhang's death does not make the omission less visible, so a compound theory-plus-experiment citation would invite the charge of an assembled prize. That is why B048 is my second alternative and not my lead. On the question you put to the B049 group, what is learned about nature, my answer is that the lattice clock shows one can keep the statistics of an ensemble with the cleanliness of a single ion, which was widely believed to be a trade-off. That is a result about what nature permits, even without an anomaly.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock changes what is achievable, not only how well an existing method performs, since it beats the single-ion signal-to-noise limit by a mechanism that did not exist before the magic-wavelength idea, and that the overlap with 2005 and 2012 is a question of framing and not eligibility.
responses.response: I agree and it is the argument I intend to carry in the committee's background text. Two cautions I would add. First, the argument works only if the citation stays on the mechanism, so I would resist wording that reads as precision metrology in general. Second, your own caveat that part of the harvest is still prospective is why I would not claim geodesy or the redefinition of the second as part of the achievement. The strength is the reproduced 1e-18 evidence, which is a measurement others have repeated, not a promise.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's contribution is part of the invention and realisation or a better execution of Katori's scheme; I cannot settle priority from the supplied material, and I would accept Katori alone only if the atomic-physics specialists judged that to be the fairer attribution.
Whether the committee accepts the boundary against the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether Danielsson's discovery-versus-instrument objection is decisive for others in the final vote.
Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second should affect the timing; I do not treat it as a precondition, but I cannot rule out that colleagues will.
Whether B024 is distinct enough from the 2015 neutrino-oscillation prize and whether the three spokesperson names can represent Daya Bay and RENO fairly, which matters only if B049 is not carried.
statement.conflict_note: I work in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur and flagged field affinity for B047 and B024 in round 1. I have now withdrawn B047, so that affinity no longer touches my preferred configuration; B024 remains only as an alternative, and I would accept recusal on it if colleagues consider it necessary. I have no direct tie to Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock groups apparent from my profile. As Chair I note that I proposed the second part in round 1 and have now dropped it on the committee's arguments, not on support counts.
